## Overview

Real comparative datasets contain many kinds of traits: body mass
(continuous), clutch size (count), migratory status (yes/no), diet type
(carnivore/herbivore/omnivore), threat status (LC < VU < EN). pigauto
handles all of them in a single model — you do not need separate
imputation runs for different column types.

### Choose a workflow

- **Fill missing cells in one trait table:** start with `impute()`. The GNN
  is off by default. Review the returned predictions and the limits for each
  trait type.
- **Inspect preprocessing, fit stages, or validation scores:** follow this
  article's lower-level workflow. Keep validation and test cells separate
  from predictions, and check each metric's scale and sample size.
- **Carry missing-data uncertainty into a downstream model:** start with the
  [multiple imputation guide](multiple-imputation.html). Choose a route that
  matches your data and analysis, then check its eligibility and validation
  limits. Random variation among completed tables alone does not establish
  valid inference.
- **Compare predictions across posterior trees:** use the
  [tree sensitivity guide](tree-uncertainty.html). This is a
  prediction-sensitivity check; tree-aware downstream inference is not
  supported by this workflow.

The mixed-type example below teaches the lower-level steps. For a first
analysis with your own data, check the species names and trait declarations
before fitting; the checklist below shows what to verify.

| Type | R class | Example | Notes |
|------|---------|---------|-------|
| Continuous | `numeric` | Body mass, wing length | Auto-detected |
| Count | `integer` | Clutch size, litter size | Auto-detected |
| Binary | `factor` (2 levels) | Migratory yes/no | Auto-detected |
| Categorical | `factor` (>2 levels) | Diet type, lifestyle | Auto-detected |
| Ordinal | `ordered` | Threat status (LC < VU < EN) | Auto-detected |
| Proportion | `numeric` (0–1) | Habitat cover, diet fraction | Requires a named override, e.g. `trait_types = c(cover = "proportion")` |
| ZI count | `integer` (zero-inflated) | Parasite load, rare behaviour | Requires a named override, e.g. `trait_types = c(parasite_load = "zi_count")`; experimental |
| Multi-proportion | K `numeric` columns summing to 1 | Diet composition, plumage-colour fractions, microbiome relative abundances | Requires `multi_proportion_groups = list(<name> = c("col1", ..., "colK"))`; encoded via centred log-ratio (CLR) + per-component z-score |

The first five rows in this table are generally inferred from R column
class, subject to the exceptions below. `proportion`, `zi_count`, and
`multi_proportion` must be declared explicitly (`trait_types` or
`multi_proportion_groups`). Two-level ordered factors are detected as binary;
integer columns with negative observed values are treated as continuous, while
other integer columns are treated as counts. Use a named `trait_types` override
when that inference does not match the measurement. All eight types share a
latent representation, but type also determines baseline eligibility and
dispatch, masking rules, loss, calibration, uncertainty summaries, and
back-transformation. For examples, see the [baseline section](#baseline-fitting)
and [prediction and decoding](#prediction-and-decoding). Names in `trait_types`
must match the corresponding trait columns.

Before fitting a mixed table, use `check_pigauto(traits, tree)`. Its trait
table records the detected type, declaration source, usable matched rows, and
copy-ready corrections; its species report distinguishes matched, data-only,
and tree-only identities.

For a real dataset, first confirm that row names (or the declared species
column) match the tree tips. Set factor levels in the intended order, explicitly
declare proportions and zero-inflated counts, and declare compositional groups
with `multi_proportion_groups`. Then resolve any issues reported by
`check_pigauto()` before fitting.

## Synthetic example

This is a teaching example with 60 simulated species, not a validation study.
The validation and test splits can contain only a few cells for some traits,
so their scores and calibration are imprecise. For a real analysis, use enough
observed values to support the validation split and inspect the reported `n`
before interpreting a score.

```{r simulate}
library(pigauto)
library(ape)

set.seed(42)
n <- 60
tree <- rtree(n)

traits <- data.frame(
  row.names = tree$tip.label,
  mass      = exp(rnorm(n, 3, 0.5)),
  clutch    = as.integer(rpois(n, 3) + 1L),
  migr      = factor(sample(c("no", "yes"), n, replace = TRUE)),
  diet      = factor(sample(c("herb", "carn", "omni"), n, replace = TRUE)),
  threat    = ordered(sample(c("LC", "VU", "EN"), n, replace = TRUE),
                      levels = c("LC", "VU", "EN"))
)
```

## Preprocessing

`preprocess_traits()` auto-detects column types from R classes:

```{r preprocess}
pd <- preprocess_traits(traits, tree)
print(pd)
```

The `trait_map` records each trait's type, levels, latent column
indices, and normalisation parameters:

```{r trait_map}
str(pd$trait_map, max.level = 1)
pd$trait_map$diet
```

## Creating splits

When `trait_map` is supplied, `make_missing_splits()` operates at the
original-trait level. For categorical traits, all K one-hot columns are held
out together. A zero-inflated count uses two latent columns: a recorded zero
has an observed zero/non-zero gate and no magnitude, while a genuinely missing
count has no observed gate. The split uses the gate to identify observed cells;
the missing magnitude for a recorded zero does not mean the raw count was
missing.

```{r splits}
spl <- make_missing_splits(pd$X_scaled, missing_frac = 0.20,
                           seed = 1, trait_map = pd$trait_map)
cat("Val cells (latent):", length(spl$val_idx), "\n")
cat("Test cells (latent):", length(spl$test_idx), "\n")
```

## Baseline fitting

The baseline depends on trait type. Continuous-family latent columns use
phylogenetic conditional multivariate-normal imputation. Discrete traits
use phylogenetic label propagation or, for eligible combinations of traits,
a threshold model. The architecture article describes the dispatch and its
fallbacks:

```{r baseline}
bl <- fit_baseline(pd, tree, splits = spl)
dim(bl$mu)
```

## Fitting

`fit_pigauto()` calibrates the phylogenetic baseline for each trait type on
validation cells. It computes conformal scores for continuous, count, ordinal,
and proportion traits, and for the positive-count magnitude of a zero-inflated
count. That last score describes magnitude conditional on a non-zero count; it
does not describe uncertainty about whether the count is zero. Binary,
categorical, and multi-proportion traits do not receive these conformal scores.
The lower-level fitter defaults to `gnn = FALSE`, so this example fits the
baseline without constructing a network. Set `gnn = TRUE` to train the GNN
correction as well. The example fixes both continuous and discrete Pagel's
lambda at 1 to keep this small illustration quick; it does not compare
lambda settings. The `impute()` convenience function also defaults to the
baseline-only route.

```{r train, message = FALSE}
fit <- fit_pigauto(
  pd, tree,
  splits = spl,
  gnn = FALSE,
  lambda_mode = "fixed_1",
  discrete_lambda = "fixed_1",
  verbose = FALSE,
  seed = 1
)
print(fit)
```

## Prediction and decoding

`predict()` decodes latent predictions back to original types:

```{r predict}
pred <- predict(fit, return_se = TRUE)
head(pred$imputed)
```

For binary and categorical traits, class probabilities are available:

```{r probs}
# Binary: probability of "yes"
head(pred$probabilities$migr)

# Categorical: probability of each diet class
head(pred$probabilities$diet)
```

The uncertainty matrix is type-dependent. Entries for binary and categorical
traits are uncertainty scores, not Gaussian standard errors or measurement
units. In this example, the ordinal `threat` column uses the threshold-joint
baseline, which currently returns zero in `pred$se`; that zero is a placeholder,
not evidence of certainty or an ordinal standard error. Continuous-family
columns have scale-specific standard errors; see the
[uncertainty guide](gnn-architecture.html#uncertainty-quantification) before using
them:

- **Class probabilities (`pred$probabilities`):** predicted probabilities for
  binary and categorical classes. Compare classes or report their
  probabilities.
- **Uncertainty scores (`pred$se` for binary or categorical traits):**
  type-specific scores, not standard errors. Use them to rank predictions by
  uncertainty; do not form a normal interval from them.
- **Model-based standard errors (`pred$se` for supported continuous-family
  traits):** values on a trait-specific scale. Check the scale and assumptions
  in the uncertainty guide; these are not conformal intervals.
- **Conformal bounds (`pred$conformal_lower` and `pred$conformal_upper`):**
  held-out residual-calibrated prediction bounds for supported traits. They
  are not Rubin-pooled uncertainty for a downstream model.

```{r se}
head(pred$se)
```

## Evaluation

`evaluate_imputation()` dispatches type-specific metrics. Use
`evaluation = TRUE` to keep validation and test values out of prediction:


```{r evaluate}
pred_eval <- predict(fit, evaluation = TRUE)
ev <- evaluate_imputation(pred_eval, pd$X_scaled, spl)
print(ev)
```

Read `split` to distinguish validation from test results and `n` for the number
of scored cells. For continuous and count traits, RMSE is on a transformed
latent scale; for zero-inflated counts, RMSE and MAE are on the original count
scale. Lower error scores and Brier scores indicate closer predictions;
higher accuracy and correlation indicate better agreement. `coverage_95` here
uses a symmetric standard-error interval on a latent scale, not the separate
conformal-bound coverage reported by `evaluate()`. `NA` means that metric is not
available for that trait and split.

## Experimental analysis-aware multiple imputation

`multi_impute_analysis()` requires the downstream formula before imputation.
The initial backend supports exactly one incomplete continuous covariate under
MAR. It does not yet impute the mixed discrete and compositional outcomes shown
earlier in this vignette for downstream inference.

This code is a template, not a standalone example. `analysis_data` must
contain a binary outcome `y`, one incomplete continuous predictor `x`, and
a fully observed continuous predictor `z`; here `model = "glm"` specifies
a binomial-logit model. For a runnable minimal example, see the
[`multi_impute_analysis()` function reference](../reference/multi_impute_analysis.html).
The [multiple-imputation guide](multiple-imputation.html) explains eligibility
and the current validation limits.

```{r mi_workflow, eval=FALSE}
# Precompute nonlinear auxiliaries explicitly when required.
analysis_data$z_sq <- analysis_data$z^2
mi <- multi_impute_analysis(
  data = analysis_data, formula = y ~ x + z,
  missing = "x", model = "glm", m = 50L,
  auxiliary = "z_sq", seed = 1L
)

# Fit a downstream model to each
fits <- with_imputations(mi, function(d) {
  glm(y ~ x + z, data = d, family = binomial)
})

# Pool with Rubin's rules
pool_mi(fits)
```

`pool_mi()` returns a tidy data.frame with `estimate`, `std.error`, `p.value`,
`df` (classical Rubin degrees of freedom by default, or Barnard-Rubin when
`df_fun` supplies complete-data residual degrees of freedom), `fmi` (fraction of missing information),
and `riv` (relative increase in variance) per coefficient.

The `"lm"` branch uses proper Bayesian normal-regression MI, `"glm"` uses
`smcfcs` for a binomial-logit model, and `"lmer"` uses `jomo.smc` for one
Gaussian random intercept. Fixed effects only: multiple incomplete columns,
missing discrete covariates, MNAR, interactions/nonlinear terms involving the
incomplete covariate, random slopes, variance components, correlations,
BLUPs/conditional modes, and latent loadings are unsupported.

For prediction diagnostics, the lower-level
`predict(fit, n_imputations = 5L)` interface returns stochastic datasets.
These are not supported for downstream inference. The analysis-aware
`multi_impute_analysis()` route admits its own narrow class of objects
to `with_imputations()` and `pool_mi()`; the posterior route from
`multi_impute()` supports the separately documented continuous-trait
analyses.

The analysis-aware backend is implemented, but implementation alone does not
establish validated inferential performance. In the registered tests, 23 of
24 method-by-scenario results were indeterminate and one binomial-logit GLM
result failed; none was classified as supported, and 12 controls used complete
data. See the [registered inferential results](validation-results.html#inferential-results)
and the [multiple-imputation guide](multiple-imputation.html) before choosing
an inferential route.
